newsitem.title: RWANDA: Countless died in Rwandan 1994 genocide.
newsitem.headline: Countless died in Rwandan 1994 genocide.

text.p: The true figure for the number of people killed in Rwanda's genocide in 1994 vanished with corpses stuffed in pit latrines, buried in mass graves and set ablaze.
Estimates range from 500,000 to one million people slaughtered across Rwanda in three months of mass bloodletting, believed to be the fastest genocide of its scale in history.
French historian Gerard Prunier by estimating the number of Tutsis in Rwanda who survived puts the number of dead at between 800,000 and 850,000, more than 10 percent of the population.
He estimated there were 930,000 Tutsis in Rwanda before the slaughter.

The genocide started minutes after the April 6 killing of Hutu President Juvenal Habyarimana when his plane, also carrying Burundi's President Cyprien Ntarymira, was hit by a rocket and crashed in Kigali.
Presidential guards fanned out in Tutsi neighbourhoods near Kigali airport and started slaughtering men, women and children while other troops killed Tutsi and Hutu moderate leaders.
The killing spread like wildfire across the country as Hutu troops were joined by Hutu militiamen armed months before the genocide and boasting they could kill 3,000 people an hour.

Local leaders gathered the Hutu population in public rallies and ordered them to kill all Tutsis and moderate Hutus. Many of those who refused were accused of cooperating with Tutsi rebels and killed.
Using the threat of a Tutsi rebellion, troops and militiamen swiftly put up thousands of roadblocks in the capital and intercepted fleeing Tutsis or suspected Tutsis and killed them.
Tutsis stopped at the checkpoints were slaughtered and their bodies were laid out until convicts in pink uniforms came and picked up the dead and loaded them into garbage trucks.
Away from the checkpoints, Hutu soldiers and militiamen roamed neighbourhoods, shooting or hacking to death anyone who ran from them and looting homes and offices.
They also searched the homes, shops and offices as they went, looking for Tutsis hiding in ceilings and septic tanks.
At Kigali Central Hospital a few days into the genocide hundreds of corpses topped by two young men still dying crying with their throats cut were piled in a mound.
Soldiers at the hospital watched for anyone who tried to remove any wounded, who were the first tossed into a garbage truck to be pinned down by hundreds of corpses.
Bands of militiamen, most of them drunk, one armed with a samurai sword and others with clubs with nails driven through them, rampaged through a poor neighborhood behind the hospital.
In the southern city of Butare, which was slow to join the frenzy of bloodletting, presidential guards arrived by plane and the local prefect was replaced. Mass killings began in hours.
Terrified Tutsi men, women and children were dragged out of their homes and thrown into large pits lined with tyres doused with petrol and set ablaze.

A Belgian businessman forced to see his Tutsi mother-in-law being tossed into one pit said rains put out the flames after several days before a local official ordered the pits covered with earth and turf to hide them from the air.

The Belgian, who escaped to neighbouring Burundi, said days later however heavy rains dislodged the earth covering one pit on a hillside and whitened limbs could clearly be seen protruding from the dirt.
